definition: In machine learning (ML), a margin classifier is a type of classification model which is able to give an associated distance from the decision boundary for each data sample.
details: For instance, if a linear classifier is used, the distance (typically Euclidean, though others may be used) of a sample from the separating hyperplane is the margin of that sample. The notion of margins is important in several ML classification algorithms, as it can be used to bound the generalization error of these classifiers. These bounds are frequently shown using the VC dimension. The generalization error bound in boosting algorithms and support vector machines is particularly prominent.

explainer.lead: A margin classifier is a classification model that gives, for each sample, an associated distance from the decision boundary. It matters because margins can bound a classifier's generalization error, notably in boosting and support vector machines.

tiers.eli5: It is like knowing not just which side of a line a point falls on, but how far it is from the line, so you can tell how confident the call is.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use margins to gauge confidence and to set training objectives that push samples away from the boundary. The pitfall is over-weighting margin without checking real error, since the bounds rely on assumptions such as the VC dimension.

explainer.example: A support vector machine reports, for each sample, its distance from the separating hyperplane, and that margin feeds a generalization error bound.
